set.t: Christ with Mary and Martha ('Consider the Lilies')
set.a: Christian Georg Hahn, after Julius Hübner

summary: Christ stands in a sunlit clearing at the centre of a gathered crowd of men, women and children, one hand open in a gesture of teaching. At the left a woman kneels beside a clump of flowers, and the Wellcome Collection explains that he is pointing to Mary with the lilies as he speaks the words 'Consider the lilies how they grow'. The calm, balanced composition, framed by an ornamental border, carries Julius Hübner's devotional painting to a wide Victorian-era public.
facts: Julius Hübner (1806–1882), a history painter of the Düsseldorf school, painted a 'Consider the Lilies' in 1839; this lithograph reproduces his composition.

The print was drawn on the stone by Christian Georg Hahn and published in Berlin by L. Sachse, with Goupil & Vibert in Paris and Hering & Remington in London as co-publishers, showing how such religious images circulated internationally.
It is a large sheet: image, lettering and border measure about 52 × 69.5 cm (Wellcome Collection 766646i).
notes: Wellcome dates the print '[between 1840 and 1849?]'; our date '184X'/year 184 was a parsing error. The Wellcome record has been merged into work gb3h2bx7.

set.t: Christ Showing His Sacred Heart (holy card)
set.m: Colour process print with shaped edges

summary: On this small devotional card Christ stands barefoot on soft clouds in a long white robe and mantle, his right hand open towards the viewer and his left pointing to the flaming heart shown on his breast. The caption reads 'Sacro Cuore di Gesù'. Wellcome identifies the figure as Christ in the form in which he appeared to St Margaret Mary Alacoque, the visionary behind the modern devotion to the Sacred Heart.
facts: The modern devotion to the Sacred Heart derives from the visions reported by the French nun Margaret Mary Alacoque between 1673 and 1675.
The card is tiny, about 10.8 × 5.8 cm, with decoratively shaped edges typical of early 20th-century holy cards (Wellcome Collection 31493i).
notes: Wellcome dates it '[between 1910 and 1919]'; our '191X'/year 191 was a parsing error. Place inferred from the Italian caption. The Wellcome record has been merged into work x234febn.

summary: Cut into a tiny oval of carnelian, a standing shepherd carries a sheep across his shoulders, holding its legs at his chest, while small animals stand at his feet. Such engraved gems were set in rings and used as seals, so the image would have been pressed into wax by its owner. In Christian hands the old pastoral motif became an image of Christ the Good Shepherd, though on a gem without Christian symbols the meaning cannot be certain.
facts: The gem is only about 1.5 cm high; Yale describes it as Roman work from Syria of the 3rd–4th century.
The ram-bearer (kriophoros) figure goes back to Greek art, where it was associated with Hermes, and was adapted by Christians as an image of Christ the Good Shepherd.
It was given to the Yale University Art Gallery in 1986 by Ambassador and Mrs William L. Eagleton, Jr.
notes: Identification uncertain: shepherds carrying sheep appear on both pagan and Christian gems, and this one shows no Christian symbol; the museum's title calls it a Good Shepherd.

summary: A young shepherd in a belted, short tunic carries a heavy-fleeced sheep across his shoulders, gripping its legs together at his chest. The figure is broken off below the knees, and a squared block rising behind the sheep shows that it once served as a support for a piece of furniture such as a table. The ram-bearer was an old pastoral type, and around A.D. 300 it was widely used by Christians as an image of Christ the Good Shepherd.
facts: The Getty records the figure as 57.5 cm high and also catalogues it under the name 'Moschophoros' (calf- or sheep-bearer).
Its recorded history begins at Rokeby Hall in Yorkshire, England, in the Morritt collection; it was sold at Sotheby's, London, on 1 July 1969.
Getty suggests it was made in the eastern provinces of the Roman Empire, with a question mark.
notes: Identification uncertain: a sheep-bearer on a furniture support may be a pastoral decoration rather than a deliberately Christian image; the Getty's title calls it a Good Shepherd.

summary: Framed by spirally fluted columns under a low pediment, a curly-haired young shepherd stands with a sheep slung over his shoulders, smiling slightly as he looks out at the viewer. Two more sheep wait at his feet beside two small trees, and a bird perches in the branches at the left. The slab is a clear, confident example of the Good Shepherd as it was carved on Christian sarcophagi around 300, promising the dead the care of the shepherd who seeks out the lost.
facts: The museum notes the shepherd's practical dress: a belted long-sleeved tunic, laced boots and puttees, wrappings that protected the legs from thorny undergrowth.
The slab was probably cut from the centre of a strigilated sarcophagus, where three relief panels were separated by wavy fluting.
It was bought by Princeton from the dealer Piero Tozzi in Rome in 1952.
notes: Museum date range 250–350 ('ca. 300 CE').

summary: At the right end of this marble fragment a youthful shepherd with thick curls carries a lamb across his shoulders, holding its legs, while two sheep look up at him from below. The rest of the surface is filled with the S-shaped fluting (strigilation) typical of Roman sarcophagi. According to the Walters, the fragment comes from a small Early Christian sarcophagus probably made for a child, for whom the image of Christ the Good Shepherd carrying his sheep home was a fitting consolation.
facts: The Walters dates the fragment to the early 4th century (300–325) and describes the sarcophagus as probably made for a child.
The museum notes that the Good Shepherd image grew out of the pagan figure of Hermes as ram-bearer before it was taken up as an image of Jesus.
It entered the Walters in 2001, purchased from Royal-Athena Galleries.

set.t: Bowl with the Raising of Lazarus

summary: Stamped reliefs are spaced across the floor of this red earthenware bowl. At the top stands Lazarus' tomb, a small temple-like shrine on a decorated base with the swaddled Lazarus upright in its doorway. A veiled woman stands at the left, and at the right a long-haired figure in a mantle stretches out a hand towards the tomb in a gesture of command, generally read as Christ calling his friend back to life; two small trees complete the scene.
facts: The Walters explains that the bowl belongs to a group of stamped terracotta objects made in North Africa as an inexpensive substitute for vessels of precious metal.
The Raising of Lazarus was one of the most popular subjects in the Roman catacombs, appearing from the 2nd century.
notes: Identification uncertain: the gesturing figure at the right lacks the wand usually held by Christ in this scene and could be read as one of Lazarus' sisters; the museum text does not identify the figures.

set.m: Free-blown glass with wheel-cut decoration; very pale green, nearly colourless

summary: Around this thin, nearly colourless beaker, wheel-cut lines build up a frieze of robed figures. Yale identifies the central pair as Lazarus, still wrapped in his burial shroud, and Jesus, holding a staff in his left hand, with four other figures who are probably onlookers. Made in the century of Constantine's conversion, it shows a Gospel miracle of resurrection entering the luxury tableware of Roman households.
facts: The decoration was made by wheel-cutting: a rotating wheel of metal or stone coated with abrasive cut shallow grooves, and groups of parallel cuts suggest anatomy, drapery and landscape. Yale associates this style with glass-cutters working in Cologne.
Although probably made in the Rhineland, the cup was found at Boulogne-sur-Mer in northern France; it was later in the collections of Engel Gross and Fahim Kouchakji.
It was shown in the Baltimore Museum of Art's 1947 exhibition 'Early Christian and Byzantine Art' (catalogue no. 625).
notes: Yale's display date is 'ca. 4th century A.D.'; its structured date field is a placeholder. 'Colorles' typo in the museum medium corrected.

summary: A red carnelian set in a simple gold ring is engraved with the Good Shepherd: a standing youth carries a sheep across his shoulders while two more sheep stand at his feet, between small trees. According to the Walters the ring also bears an anchor with a Christian monogram on one side and a vine on the other, marking it clearly as a Christian's possession. Pressed into wax as a seal, the image proclaimed its owner's trust in Christ the shepherd.
facts: The ring was once owned by the archaeologist Sir Arthur Evans (his inventory no. 219) and was said to come from Catania in Sicily.
After Evans's death it passed through his executor Jacob Hirsch to Saidie A. May, who gave it to the Walters in 1942.
notes: The anchor and vine described by the museum are not visible in the frontal photograph. Date: 4th century (museum).

reject_reason: Not a depiction of Christ: a plain two-handled earthenware jug ('Punic urn') dated c. 400 BC; it was matched only because the Dutch title contains 'vóór Christus' (BC).
Not a depiction: a text-only page of the Coptic Manichaean Psalm-book (a psalm addressed to Jesus); no image of Christ.
Not a depiction: text-only pages (Psalms of Jesus 252–254) from the Coptic Manichaean Psalm-book; no image of Christ.
Not a depiction: text-only pages (psalms to the Trinity and to Christ) from the Coptic Manichaean Psalm-book; no image of Christ.
Christ is not depicted: the lamp's discus shows only the shrouded Lazarus standing in the doorway of his gabled tomb (as the Walters' own description says), without the figure of Christ.
notes: A 5th-century North African-type terracotta lamp; the Lazarus image alone stands for the miracle.

set.t: Lamp with Christ Triumphant

summary: On the round discus of this North African red-slip lamp stands a single frontal figure holding a long cross, flanked by the two filling holes, while a ring of small stamped motifs runs around the shoulder. Princeton identifies the figure as Christ triumphant, a victorious image that suited a lamp: the light of the flame may have recalled Christ as the light of the world. Such lamps were made in great numbers in the workshops of Roman Tunisia.
facts: The lamp is made of African red slip ware, the fine orange-red pottery of Roman North Africa, and Princeton dates it to the second half of the 5th century.
It was bought by the museum from Geledakis in Paris in August 1923.
It was lent to the 1947 Baltimore exhibition 'Early Christian and Byzantine Art' (no. 633) and shown again in 'Byzantium at Princeton' in 1986 (no. 135).
notes: The figure is small and worn in the photograph; details such as beasts beneath the feet, common on this lamp type, cannot be confirmed.

set.t: Pendant Amulet with the Holy Rider and Christ Crucified

summary: This small, oval bronze pendant has a loop for hanging. On one side, roughly incised, a haloed figure in a long robe stands against a cross with arms outstretched, which the Walters identifies as Christ crucified. On the other, a rider on horseback spears a figure lying beneath the horse, framed by an inscription band. Worn on the body, the pairing of the holy horseman with the Crucifixion called on Christ's victory for the wearer's protection.
facts: The pendant is only about 5 × 2.3 cm; the Walters bought it from Simon Bendall, London, in 1991.
notes: Date 5th–6th century per the museum (its CSV begin-year '-499' is an error). The incised Crucifixion is very schematic; the robe and halo are visible but no inscription can be read in the photographs.

reject_reason: Not Christian: an ink rubbing of an Eastern Han dynasty (25–220) tomb relief showing horses and chariots; the museum title 'Calvary' is evidently a misspelling of 'Cavalry'.

set.c: Seleucia Pieria (port of Antioch), now Turkey

summary: Only part of a face survives on this broken marble slab: a long straight nose, the line of a moustache, the mouth and the start of a beard, carved in shallow relief beside broad roughened areas. Princeton identifies it as an icon of Christ from the decoration of a four-apsed (tetraconch) church. Even as a fragment it is an early witness to the bearded, frontal image of Christ in the churches of Byzantine Syria.
facts: It was excavated by the Princeton-led expedition to Antioch-on-the-Orontes (1931–1939) at Seleucia, Antioch's port, and has been in the museum since 1939.
It was published by Richard Stillwell in 'Antioch-on-the-Orontes III: The Excavations 1937–1939' (1941), pl. 25, no. 460.
notes: Identification rests on the museum's title; the surviving features are consistent with a bearded Christ but are fragmentary. Museum display date ca. 490–550. Scripture omitted.

summary: A bronze bowl-shaped censer still hangs from a length of its twisted chain. Around its body are round medallions with busts in relief; the one turned to the front shows Christ with a cross-marked halo, between stylised plant ornaments. As incense smoke rose from it during the liturgy, the faces of Christ, the Virgin and the apostles circled the worshippers.
facts: The Getty describes four medallions: Christ, Saint Peter, the Virgin Mary and probably Saint Paul.
Three suspension loops survive, one only partly, with four and a half links of one length of twisted S-shaped chain; the censer is 10 cm high.
It was given to the Getty in 1979 by Lee Rizzuto.
notes: Date 6th–7th century per museum.

summary: This small gold ring has an octagonal hoop, each facet engraved and inlaid with black niello with a scene from the life of Christ. On the oval bezel the Ascension is shown in two registers: above, Christ sits in a mandorla carried up by angels, while below the Virgin stands among the apostles, who look up. Worn on the hand, the ring formed what the Walters calls 'a prayer in pictures'.
facts: The Walters notes that the ring's eight Gospel scenes were thought to have protective power, together forming a prayer in pictures.
An inscription around it quotes Isaiah 6:3, the angels' hymn: 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts'.
notes: Date 6th–7th century per the Walters (Commons gives 6th century).

set.t: Pilgrim Token with the Virgin and Child

summary: This small disc of fired clay is pressed with a worn image of the Virgin enthroned, holding the Christ Child on her lap, between two flanking figures, perhaps angels, under a raised border. As its museum title indicates, it is a pilgrim's token, a humble keepsake carried home from a journey to a holy place.
facts: The Walters bought the token from Simon Bendall, London, in 1991, and attributes it to Syria.
notes: Identification uncertain only in detail: the Virgin's seated figure is clear in the old black-and-white photograph, but the Child is barely legible. Date 6th–7th century per museum.

summary: The round bezel of this bronze ring, edged with a beaded border, shows a figure riding sideways on a donkey towards the right, with a small cross set in the field above. Princeton identifies the scene as Christ's Entry into Jerusalem. Rings with Gospel scenes like this were worn as signs of faith and protection by ordinary Christians of the Byzantine East.
facts: Princeton dates the ring to the 6th–7th century and attributes it to the eastern Mediterranean; it is only 2.3 cm across.
It was given to the museum in 1968 by Rev. Dr Adolph H. Behrenberg and was shown in the exhibition 'Byzantium at Princeton' in 1986 (no. 95).

set.t: Christ in Majesty with the Virgin, John the Evangelist, Saints and a Kneeling Monk (leaf from the Speculum Virginum)
set.a: Unknown illuminator (text attributed to Conrad of Hirsau)

summary: At the top of the page Christ sits on a rainbow in a green-bordered mandorla against a blue ground, blessing with his right hand and holding an open book. Crowds of saints stand on either side, among them the Virgin and John the Evangelist, and below a tonsured monk kneels and stretches up a scroll towards Christ's feet. The lively pen drawing, lightly coloured, introduces a text written for the instruction of religious women.
facts: The manuscript was written at the Cistercian abbey of Himmerode in Germany in the early 13th century; an erased 15th-century ownership note names the monks of Himmerode.

The Speculum Virginum ('Mirror of Virgins') is a 12th-century dialogue between a teacher, Peregrinus, and a student, Theodora, on the religious life of women; its authorship is uncertain, with Conrad of Hirsau one proposed author.
The Walters describes its copy as one of twenty-two surviving Latin manuscripts of the text, with twelve illustrations.
notes: Museum date 1200–1225; the 7th-century date in our data was an import error. The Walters credits Conrad of Hirsau as author of the text, not as artist.

set.t: Solidus of Justinian II with the Bust of Christ

summary: On the face of this gold coin Christ appears as a bust with long hair and a full beard, a cross behind his head, raising his right hand in blessing and holding the book of the Gospels. The legend names him 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. On the reverse the emperor stands in consular robes holding a cross on steps, with the title 'servant of Christ', so the coin itself declares who is the true sovereign.
facts: Justinian II was the first Byzantine emperor to put the image of Christ on coins issued in his name; this long-haired type belongs to his first reign (685–695).
Yale records the legends as IHSUS XRISTUS REX REGNANTIUM on the obverse and IUSTINIANUS SERVUS XRISTI on the reverse, with the mint mark COMOB.
The coin weighs 4.43 g and was struck at Constantinople; it came to Yale from Professor Alfred R. Bellinger.
notes: A different specimen of the same type as other Justinian II solidi in the collection, not a duplicate object.

summary: This squat bronze censer is cast all round with crowded scenes in relief, separated by palm-like trees, and a band of leafy scrolls runs round the rim. The Walters identifies the Annunciation, Nativity, Crucifixion and the Women at the Tomb on the sides, while on the underside the Virgin sits enthroned holding the Christ Child. Swung in the liturgy, it wrapped the story of Christ's life, death and resurrection in clouds of incense.
facts: The Walters explains that incense, blessed and burned on coals inside such censers, was believed to carry prayers up to heaven, and that its ingredients such as frankincense, myrrh and aloeswood were thought to purify.
The Walters attributes the censer to Syria and dates it to the 7th–8th century.
It was given to the museum in 1981 by Mrs Carol L. Brewster.
notes: The museum's culture field reads 'Eastern Orthodox'; style set to Byzantine, following the museum's description of it as a Byzantine censer.

set.t: Deposition and Flagellation (diptych leaf)

summary: Two scenes of the Passion are stacked on this small ivory leaf. Above, Joseph of Arimathea embraces the body of Christ as it is lowered from the cross, while the Virgin takes his hanging arm and another mourner stands at the left; below, Christ stands bound to a column between two tormentors who raise their scourges. The open compositions and large figures give the little panel a monumental quality.
facts: The Walters assigns the leaf to the 'Rose Group' of French Gothic ivories, named after the rosettes on their mouldings, as seen here.
The museum notes two unusual features: a single element of landscape beneath the feet of one tormentor, and roped sides not found on other examples of the group.
notes: Museum date 1301–1325; the 8th-century date in our data was an import error. The hinges show it was one wing of a diptych.

reject_reason: Not Christ: a Maya plate (600–800) showing the maize god Jun Ixiim re-emerging from the underworld; matched only because the title contains 'resurrection'.

set.t: Processional Cross with Mosaic Head of Christ and Chi-Rho
set.m: Copper with mosaic inlay, on a modern wooden base

summary: This copper cross has four flaring arms with moulded ends, set on a short stepped shaft. The photograph shows the reverse, where a small mosaic panel on a blue ground carries the Chi-Rho monogram of Christ with the letters alpha and omega. According to Castle Huis Bergh, the front holds a matching, very fine mosaic of the head of Christ, so the cross would have carried both his name and his face in procession.
facts: The castle's catalogue describes the cross as shaped like a St Andrew's cross, a square with deeply scooped sides whose corners end in feet, standing on a short heavy shaft.
It notes that a small piece of the mosaic beside the head of Christ is missing.
notes: Identification uncertain: the head of Christ is described by the museum but is on the side not shown in the image, which shows only the Chi-Rho. The 6th–7th-century date comes from the museum record and could not be independently verified; micromosaic decoration on such a cross is unusual, and the date should be treated with caution.

reject_reason: Not Christ: a Maya tripod plate (600–800) with a maize-god resurrection scene; matched only because the title contains 'resurrection'.

summary: Carved from a tall curved section of tusk, this ivory shows the Virgin seated with the Christ Child on her lap; he throws his arm round her neck and presses his cheek to hers, while she gazes straight ahead with large, fixed eyes. At the right a standing attendant holds a staff, and a small face appears in the upper corner. The Walters calls it one of the earliest examples of the tender embrace later known in Byzantium as the Eleousa, or Virgin of Tenderness.
facts: The museum suggests the relief was an icon for private devotion, in a monastic or domestic setting, and singles out the large head, fixed gaze and angular drapery as typical of early medieval Christian Egypt.
It is unusually large for an ivory, about 26 cm high, its shape following the curve of the tusk.
It was in Cologne in the 1870s and passed through two Paris sales before Henry Walters bought it in 1905.
notes: Date 7th–8th century per the Walters (Commons gives 7th century).

set.t: Head of Christ (carved bean pod)
set.d: undated (after the Spanish conquest; probably 18th–19th century)
set.m: Carved bean pod in a dark mount

summary: Within a tiny dark mount, a carver has cut the head of Christ from a seed pod: the face is long and calm, framed by finely worked curling hair and a forked beard, with a thin band across the brow that may be the crown of thorns. The minute scale and naturalistic, European-style features make it a remarkable piece of devotional miniature work from South America.
facts: The carving is only about 3 × 2.6 cm.
Princeton records it as South American and probably a gift of Elroy Curtis (Class of 1900), from the collection of William E. Curtis.
notes: The museum gives no date (its date range is 1–1954); the 'A.D. 500–1000' in our data is unfounded. The European iconography means it cannot predate the Spanish conquest, and the style suggests the 18th or 19th century; year 1850 is an approximate placeholder. Scripture omitted.

set.a: Master of Walters 185 (miniatures); scribe Johannes de Malborch
set.m: Ink, paint and gold on parchment
set.t: Christ Carrying the Cross

summary: Against a chequered ground of gold, blue and red, Christ in a purple robe and crown of thorns stoops under a great wooden cross as he walks to the left. Soldiers in short tunics press round him, while the Virgin and John follow in grief at the back. The full-page miniature, framed by delicate sprays of gold ivy, opens a section of the prayers on Christ's Passion.
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.
notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error.

set.a: Master of Walters 185 (miniatures); scribe Johannes de Malborch
set.m: Ink, paint and gold on parchment
set.t: The Crucifixion

summary: Christ hangs on the cross beneath a titulus, his thin pale body bleeding from his wounds and his head bowed, against a patterned ground of gold and blue. The Virgin, wrapped in a deep blue mantle, stands at the left with her hand to her face, and John, in red, holds a book at the right. The miniature is set in a wide margin of gold ivy sprays.
facts: The book was probably made for a married couple who were originally painted kneeling with scrolls and coats of arms in the margins flanking this Crucifixion; their figures and arms were later erased and overpainted with white.
The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.
notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error.

set.a: Master of Walters 185 (miniatures); scribe Johannes de Malborch
set.m: Ink, paint and gold on parchment
set.t: The Entombment

summary: The body of Christ, still wearing the crown of thorns, is laid in a pink stone sarcophagus by two men, one at his head and one at his feet. Behind the tomb the Virgin in blue joins her hands in prayer, and John in red bows his head beside her, all set against a chequered gold ground. The quiet, tender scene closes the cycle of the Passion in this book of prayers.
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.
notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error.

set.a: Master of Walters 185 (miniatures); scribe Johannes de Malborch
set.m: Ink, paint and gold on parchment
set.t: The Flagellation

summary: Christ stands bound to a slender pink column, naked except for a loincloth, his body marked with wounds. Two tormentors in brightly coloured tunics and hose lunge at him from either side with raised scourges, their twisting poses contrasting with his stillness. The black-and-white chequered floor and patterned gold ground give the small scene a jewel-like intensity.
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.
notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error.

set.t: Gem with the Crucifixion

summary: Moulded in banded red glass in imitation of a precious stone, this small oval shows Christ on the cross, his body swaying slightly and his head inclined within a halo, between the Virgin at the left and John at the right. Above the arms of the cross are the Greek abbreviations IC XC, 'Jesus Christ'. The use of the Greek monogram points to Byzantine models, made affordable in glass for personal devotion.
facts: The gem measures only 2.5 × 2 cm.
It was given to Princeton by Mrs Albert E. McVitty and published among the museum's recent acquisitions in 1955.
notes: Princeton gives no display date, only the broad range 400–1499 and the label 'Medieval'; the 'A.D. 500–1000' in our data is unsupported. The swaying body and the Virgin-and-John composition suggest Middle Byzantine models (10th century or later), but no firm date can be given; year 950 is a midpoint placeholder.

set.a: Master of Walters 185 (miniatures); scribe Johannes de Malborch
set.m: Ink, paint and gold on parchment
set.t: Initial D with the Virgin and Child

summary: Inside a gilded initial D, the Virgin in a deep blue mantle holds the Christ Child close against her cheek. The initial opens the Hours of the Virgin, under the red heading 'Hore de domina nostra', and the page is framed by a rich border of gold and coloured foliage inhabited by small creatures. It is an intimate image placed at the start of the most-used prayers of the book.
scripture: Psalm 51:15 (text on the page: 'Domine labia mea aperies')
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.

set.a: Master of Walters 185 (miniatures); scribe Johannes de Malborch
set.m: Ink, paint and gold on parchment
set.t: The Lamentation

summary: At the foot of the empty cross the Virgin, in a lilac mantle, cradles the dead Christ across her lap, while John in an orange-red mantle kneels behind and lifts his limp arm. Their haloed heads lean together against a gold and blue lattice ground. The miniature invites the reader to share the grief of Christ's mother and friend.
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.

set.a: Master of Walters 185 (miniatures); scribe Johannes de Malborch
set.m: Ink, paint and gold on parchment
set.t: The Last Judgment

summary: Christ the Judge sits on a rainbow above the earth, his arms spread to show his wounds and his body wrapped in a pink mantle. The Virgin at the left and a saint in red at the right intercede, while below them small naked figures of the dead climb out of the ground. Placed in a book of personal prayers, the scene reminded its owners of the judgment for which they prayed to be ready.
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.
notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error. The saint at the right is probably John the Baptist or John the Evangelist; not identified by the museum.

set.t: Initial D with the Fool before Christ (leaf from the Psalter of Jernoul de Camphaing)

summary: Inside a pink initial D on a gold ground, a fool carrying a staff or club confronts Christ, who stands at the right in a blue mantle with a halo, raising his hand. The initial opens Psalm 52 in the Latin numbering, 'Dixit insipiens in corde suo: non est Deus' ('The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God'), so the painter shows the fool face to face with the God he denies. Delicate pen flourishes in red and blue run down the margin.
facts: The psalter was made for Jernoul de Camphaing, whose name appears in a red inscription in the book (fol. 226r); the Walters places it in northeastern France, c. 1250–1275.

In illuminated psalters, historiated initials marked the beginnings of the major divisions of the Psalms and helped readers find their place in books without page numbers; Psalm 52 began one such division.
The manuscript was owned by the Paris binder and collector Léon Gruel before Henry Walters acquired it.
notes: Museum date 1250–1275; the 8th-century date in our data was an import error. Psalm 52 as a division opening is standard in the eightfold liturgical division of the Psalter.

set.t: Initial D with King David Pointing to His Eyes before Christ (leaf from the Psalter of Jernoul de Camphaing)

summary: Within a blue initial D on a gold ground, the crowned King David stands at the left and points to his eyes, while Christ, haloed and robed in red and blue, stands facing him at the right. The initial opens Psalm 26 in the Latin numbering, 'Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea' ('The Lord is my light and my salvation'), and David's gesture shows that it is Christ who gives him sight. Red and blue penwork flourishes frame the text.
facts: The opening words of the psalm, 'Dominus illuminatio mea', are legible beside the initial, followed by 'Dominus protector vite mee a quo trepidabo'.
In illuminated psalters, historiated initials marked the beginnings of the major divisions of the Psalms; Psalm 26 (Latin numbering) began one of these divisions.
The psalter was made for Jernoul de Camphaing, named in a red inscription on fol. 226r.
notes: Museum date 1250–1275; the 8th-century date in our data was an import error.
